title: Chapter 5 Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of clustering fundamentals, K‑Means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, and evaluation!

questions.question: What is the primary goal of clustering?
options: To group similar data points without labels
questions.explanation: Clustering is unsupervised; it groups data based on similarity without predefined labels.

questions.question: In K‑Means, what does a centroid represent?
options: A data point that is misclassified
The mean position of all points in a cluster
questions.explanation: Centroids are the averages (means) of the points assigned to each cluster.

questions.question: How does the elbow method help in K‑Means?
options: It automatically chooses the best features
It determines the optimal number of clusters by locating a bend in the inertia plot
questions.explanation: The elbow method looks for the k where adding more clusters yields diminishing returns in inertia reduction.

questions.question: Which linkage method in hierarchical clustering tends to produce the most compact clusters?
questions.explanation: Complete linkage uses the farthest neighbour distance, forcing clusters to be compact.

questions.question: Ward’s method minimises the total within‑cluster variance.
questions.explanation: True. Ward’s merges clusters that lead to the smallest increase in the sum of squared errors.

questions.question: In DBSCAN, what is a noise point?
options: A point that is the centre of a dense region
A point that has fewer than MinPts neighbours within ε and is not near any core point
A point that belongs to multiple clusters
A point with the highest silhouette score
questions.explanation: Noise points are outliers; they are not dense enough to be core nor reachable from a core point.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of DBSCAN over K‑Means?
options: It can find arbitrarily shaped clusters and detect outliers
It works better with high‑dimensional data
questions.explanation: DBSCAN excels at arbitrary shapes and noise detection; K‑Means struggles with non‑spherical shapes.

questions.question: What does ε (epsilon) control in DBSCAN?
options: The minimum number of points per cluster
The radius of the neighbourhood around a point
questions.explanation: ε defines the maximum distance for two points to be considered neighbours.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of the basic DBSCAN algorithm?
options: It cannot find clusters of varying density well with a single global ε
It requires the number of clusters as input
questions.explanation: Global ε may fail when clusters have very different densities. Variants like OPTICS address this.

questions.question: Which statement about the silhouette score is correct?
options: A score near +1 means clusters are well separated and cohesive
questions.explanation: Silhouette is between -1 and 1; higher is better. It uses only the data itself (internal metric).

questions.question: How is the silhouette score for a single point computed?
questions.explanation: s(i) = (b(i) - a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i)), where a is intra‑cluster distance, b is nearest‑cluster distance.

questions.question: What is the Davies‑Bouldin index measuring?
options: The average distance between cluster centroids
The average similarity between each cluster and its most similar cluster (lower is better)
questions.explanation: DB index averages worst‑case cluster similarities; lower values indicate better clustering.

questions.question: Feature scaling is unnecessary for clustering algorithms because they are unsupervised.
questions.explanation: False. Distance‑based algorithms (K‑Means, hierarchical, DBSCAN) rely on distances; unscaled features distort clusters.

questions.question: Which clustering method is most likely to produce a dendrogram?
questions.explanation: Hierarchical methods build a tree representation; dendrograms visualise the merging process.

questions.question: In agglomerative clustering, how many clusters are there at the start?
options: As many as the number of data points
questions.explanation: Agglomerative starts with each point as its own cluster, then merges.

questions.question: Which of the following is a good first step to determine ε for DBSCAN?
options: Use the elbow method on inertia
Plot a k‑distance graph and look for an elbow
Set ε to the mean of all pairwise distances
questions.explanation: The k‑distance graph (sorted distances to k‑th neighbour) helps find a suitable ε at the knee point.

questions.question: What does `n_init` parameter in KMeans do?
options: Number of times K‑Means is run with different centroid seeds; the best result is kept
Specifies the number of nearest neighbours
questions.explanation: `n_init` runs the algorithm multiple times with different random initialisations to avoid local minima.

questions.question: A silhouette score of -0.2 suggests the clustering is excellent.
questions.explanation: Negative silhouette indicates that points might be in wrong clusters; closer to +1 is good.

questions.question: Which clustering algorithm can mark some points as not belonging to any cluster?
questions.explanation: DBSCAN explicitly labels sparse points as noise (label = -1).

questions.question: Why might you prefer hierarchical clustering over K‑Means?
options: It is faster on large datasets
You need a tree representation and don't want to pre‑specify k
questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering provides a dendrogram and allows cutting at any level to obtain different numbers of clusters.

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of standard K‑Means per iteration?
options: O(n * k * d)  (n samples, k clusters, d dimensions)
questions.explanation: Each iteration computes distances from n points to k centroids, each distance calculation O(d). So O(nkd).

questions.question: Which internal validation metric can be used to compare different clustering solutions on the same data?
questions.explanation: Accuracy, precision, recall need ground truth. Silhouette only uses the data and cluster assignments.
